metadata.title: Are only children always better? Testing the sibling effects on academic performance in rural Chinese adolescents

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a locally administered, school-based Grade 9 sample from rural areas in a single Chinese city (Guangxi province) and administered the PISA 2015 Math/Reading/Science tests as a term exam. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights or any ILSA-style sampling weights; it instead describes matched sampling within classes and subsequent regression/2SLS estimation. Because no weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (BRR/jackknife) are mentioned, weighting cannot be confirmed and the analysis should be treated as unweighted or weight-omitted. The analytic sample was constructed by selecting Grade 9 classes from participating schools and then matching each only child with a non-only peer from the same class/school/region; missing data were assessed using Mean Completer.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study targeted rural students in Grade 9 from 102 rural junior secondary schools in a single city in Guangxi province. All Grade 9 classes in each participating school were selected, then students were sampled via matched sampling: 156 only children were identified and recruited, and for each only child a non-only peer with siblings was randomly sampled from the same class, school, and region to form matched dyads. The final analytic sample comprised 312 students (156 only children and 156 non-only children). Missing data were analyzed using Mean Completer, and the paper reports regression analyses on the resulting dataset.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Grade 9 (China, rural city term exam) Math
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS: Only Child β = −0.114 (p < .05), R² = 0.315, F = 15.40***. 2SLS: Only Child β = −0.195 (p > .05), R² = 0.314. Hierarchical (Step 5): Only Child β = −0.114 (p < .05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Grade 9 (China, rural city term exam) Math the study leveraged singleton status, gender, eyesight, family SES, and parents’ academic expectation to predict math achievement, finding that singleton status had a negative association with math in OLS and hierarchical regression but became non-significant under the 2SLS instrumental-variable specification. This indicates that rural only children may be disadvantaged in math, yet the causal interpretation is limited because the IV estimate does not confirm a statistically robust effect.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Grade 9 (China, rural city term exam) Reading
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS: Eyesight β = −0.133 (p < .05), PAE β = 0.306***, KG level β = 0.194***, Reading Time β = 0.107*; Only Child β = −0.092 (not significant). 2SLS: Only Child β = −0.039 (p > .05); Reading Time β = 0.129 (p > .05). Hierarchical (Step 5): Only Child β = −0.092 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Grade 9 (China, rural city term exam) Reading the study leveraged eyesight, parents’ academic expectation, kindergarten level, leisure reading time, and desk ownership to predict reading achievement, finding that only-child status was not a significant predictor in OLS or 2SLS while PAE and early schooling (KG level) showed positive associations. This indicates that improving parental academic expectations and early childhood learning conditions may be more actionable for reading outcomes than focusing solely on sibling status, especially in rural contexts.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Grade 9 (China, rural city term exam) Science
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS: Eyesight β = −0.170**; PAE β = 0.347***; KG level β = 0.198***; Reading Time β = 0.196***; Only Child β = −0.071 (not significant). 2SLS: Only Child β = −0.071 (p > .05); Reading Time β = 0.235***. Hierarchical (Step 5): Only Child β = −0.071 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Grade 9 (China, rural city term exam) Science the study leveraged eyesight, parents’ academic expectation, kindergarten level, leisure reading time, and desk ownership to predict science achievement, finding that only-child status was not significant in OLS or 2SLS while eyesight had a negative association and PAE/KG level/reading time had positive associations. This indicates that rural science performance may be improved through health/vision support and strengthening home and early learning environments rather than through sibling-status interventions alone.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a matched rural Grade 9 sample from 102 schools in a single city in Guangxi, China, administering the Chinese version of PISA 2015 Math, Reading, and Science as a term exam. Academic outcomes were converted to standardized z scores using an IRT-based scoring approach with PISA difficulty parameters. The paper does not apply machine learning; instead it uses OLS and a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variable strategy, plus hierarchical regression robustness checks. Across outcomes, only-child status showed a negative association with math in OLS (β = −0.114, p < .05) but was not significant in 2SLS (β = −0.195, p > .05), while reading and science were not significantly predicted by only-child status in the IV models. Key positive predictors included parents’ academic expectation and kindergarten level, and eyesight was consistently negatively related to achievement. Limitations include the cross-sectional design, self-reported covariates, and the lack of reported complex survey weighting.
